title: The Feature That Was 100% Correlated With the Answer — Because It Was the Answer
partialText:
Inside the Python Data Stack — Part 7

A deep dive into data leakage across categories, time, entities, and train/test splits and how to stop your model from cheating.

Here’s a feature engineering bug worse than anything in this series so far, because it doesn’t just produce a wrong number — it produces a model that looks great in validation and then falls apart the moment it sees production data. No error. No warning. Usually a promotion, actually, right before the collapse.

segment_means = df.groupby('user_segment')['converted'].mean()
df['segment_encoded'] = df['user_segment'].map(segment_means)

Ordinary-looking target encoding: for each category, replace it with the average outcome for that category. Now check what happens for any category that only shows up once in your data — which, with enough categories, is nearly guaranteed to happen somewhere:

user_segment  converted  segment_encoded
3        seg_192          0              0.0
8        seg_277          1              1.0
38       seg_202          1              1.0
91        seg_23          0              0.0
match = (singleton_rows['converted'] == singleton_rows['segment_encoded']).mean()
fraction of singleton rows where the encoded feature exactly equals the label: 100.00%

Every single one. Not “correlated with” — equal to. The mean of one number is that number, so for any category that appears exactly once, “the average outcome for this category” and “this row’s actual outcome” are the same value by definition. You’ve built a feature that contains the answer, handed it to a model, and the model will happily learn “when this feature says 1, predict 1” — a rule that’s perfect on data built this way and worthless on anything new.

(Environment for this post: Python 3.12.3, pandas 3.0.2, NumPy 2.4.4, same sandbox as the rest of this series. Methodology: minimum of several repeated perf_counter runs where timing is relevant — most of this post is about correctness, not speed, so the numbers that matter here are correlations and match rates, not milliseconds.)

The pattern underneath all of this

Every example in this post is the same shape: compute a statistic — a mean, a lag, a rolling average — using information the model isn’t supposed to have yet, and hand it over as if it were an innocent input feature. It always looks fine. The DataFrame has no error column. It’s specifically dangerous because it looks fine, all the way through training, right up until the model meets data it couldn’t cheat on.

Here’s the whole pattern laid out at once — the rule everything in this post breaks, plus the two numbers above shown side by side with their fixes:

Leakage across time: rolling windows that see the future

Suppose you’re building a feature to help predict target, and you write:

df['rolling_mean'] = df['target'].rolling(5).mean()

This includes the current row in its own rolling average — a window of 5 ending at row i includes row i. On pure random noise with no real structure at all:

df['rolling_mean_leaky'] = df['target'].rolling(5).mean()
df['rolling_mean_correct'] = df['target'].shift(1).rolling(5).mean()
df['target'].corr(df['rolling_mean_leaky'])     # 0.452
df['target'].corr(df['rolling_mean_correct'])   # 0.015

The “leaky” version shows a 0.45 correlation with the target — on data I generated with np.random.rand, which has zero actual relationship between any of its values. That correlation is entirely manufactured: the target contributes one-fifth of the weight to its own "predictive" feature, so of course it correlates. The fixed version — shift(1) before rolling, so the window only ever sees strictly past values — drops to 0.015, which is what an honest "no real signal here" result looks like. If you've ever built a time-series feature and been surprised by how well it worked, this is worth checking before you trust it: rolling() on its own doesn't know your target is the thing you're trying to predict, and it will happily include today's answer in today's feature unless you shift first.

Leakage across entities: the shift that bleeds between customers

Related bug, different mechanism. Multiple time series stacked in one DataFrame — customers, sensors, stores — and a naive .shift():

df['prev_spend_wrong'] = df['spend'].shift(1)
    customer_id day  spend  prev_spend_wrong
0           A    1   10.0               NaN
1           A    2   12.0              10.0
2           A    3   14.0              12.0
3           B    1  500.0              14.0   <-- customer A's day-3 spend
4           B    2  505.0             500.0
5           B    3  510.0             505.0

Customer B’s first row gets customer A’s last value as its “previous spend.” Plausible-looking number, completely wrong customer. The fix is grouping before shifting:

df['prev_spend_correct'] = df.groupby('customer_id')['spend'].shift(1)

which correctly gives customer B’s first row a NaN — there genuinely is no previous spend for a customer's first appearance, and pretending otherwise with a neighboring customer's data is worse than admitting the value is missing. This is the same failure shape as the merge explosion from Part 6: a real DataFrame operation, doing exactly what it's documented to do, producing something wrong because a boundary you were relying on — "each customer's data stays together" — was never actually enforced by anything.

Leakage across train and test: the fix, and what the fix costs you

Fitting a target encoding on the whole dataset guarantees the singleton-leak problem above. Fitting it on train only fixes the leak — but introduces a real, separate issue you need to handle:

segment_means_train = train.groupby('user_segment')['converted'].mean()
test['segment_encoded'] = test['user_segment'].map(segment_means_train)
test rows whose segment never appeared in train (encoding = NaN, needs a fallback): 8 / 200

Categories that exist in test but never showed up in train get NaN — pandas has genuinely never seen that category and has nothing to encode it with, which is the correct, honest outcome, not a bug to work around by pretending you know something you don't. The usual fix is a fallback: fill those NaNs with the overall training mean, which is a reasonable prior for "a category I know nothing about." What you should not do is go back to computing the encoding on the combined data to make the NaNs disappear — that's not fixing the gap, it's reintroducing the leak you just removed in order to avoid dealing with it.

The same pattern applies to something as simple as filling missing values with a mean:

global_mean = df['value'].mean()          # peeks at test
train_mean = train['value'].mean()        # doesn't
mean using the full dataset (test included): 49.9581
mean using train only:                        48.9938

On this dataset the gap is under a point, because it’s one big random sample with no real distribution shift between train and test. That’s exactly why this kind of leakage is dangerous rather than obviously broken: on well-behaved data it barely moves anything, so it survives code review, survives a quick sanity check, and only actually costs you when train and test genuinely differ — which, in real deployments where “test” eventually means “the future,” they always eventually do. The rule that avoids all three of these leaks at once is the same rule, applied consistently: split first, then fit every statistic — means, encodings, scalers, anything — on the training partition alone, and only ever apply it, never refit it, on validation or test data.

A smaller, sharper-edged dtype note

One more thing worth knowing while you’re filling missing values: introducing NaN into an integer column silently upcasts it to float64 by default, the same class of dtype surprise from Part 5.

pd.Series([1, 2, 3, np.nan]).dtype        # float64

If you need to keep integer semantics — an ID column, a count — pandas has a nullable integer dtype that doesn’t force the upcast:

pd.Series([1, 2, 3, None], dtype='Int64').dtype   # Int64 (capital I)
0       1
1       2
2       3
3    <NA>
dtype: Int64

Note the capital I — Int64 is pandas' nullable extension type, a genuinely different thing from NumPy's lowercase int64from Part 1, and it uses pd.NA instead of np.nan to mark the gap. It's a small thing, but "this ID column silently became a float column and now has decimal points in a CSV export" is a real, mildly embarrassing bug that a one-word dtype annotation avoids entirely.

Where this goes next

Every technique in this post has been about making sure a feature only knows what it’s honestly allowed to know. Part 8 picks this up directly: scikit-learn’s Pipeline and ColumnTransformer exist largely to enforce the split-then-fit discipline from this post automatically, so that "did I accidentally fit this on data it shouldn't have seen" stops being something you have to remember and starts being something the tooling makes structurally difficult to get wrong.

title: How Family Offices Can Use Claude + FMP MCP to Detect Portfolio Drift Before Rebalancing
partialText:
A practical Claude + FMP MCP workflow for measuring allocation drift, spotting positions that have moved away from target weights, and prioritizing rebalancing review.

A portfolio rarely stays at its original allocation for long. Even without any trades, differences in stock performance gradually change position weights and can push the portfolio away from the allocation a family office originally intended.

That drift is not automatically a problem. Small deviations are normal. The more useful question is whether any holding or sector has moved far enough from its target weight to deserve closer review before a rebalancing decision is considered.

This is where Claude, connected to the Financial Modeling Prep MCP server, can help. By combining target portfolio weights with FMP historical price data and company classifications, Claude can reconstruct how a no-trade portfolio would have evolved and measure the resulting allocation drift.

In this article, we start with a hypothetical $1 million family-office portfolio established on January 2, 2026, and use FMP data through August 26, 2026 to compare target weights with reconstructed current weights. The goal is not to tell the family office what to buy or sell, but to identify which positions have moved materially away from target and which deviations deserve analyst attention before any rebalancing decision.

Why Portfolio Drift Matters Before Rebalancing

Portfolio drift happens when market movements change the weight of individual holdings even though the family office has made no trades.

Suppose a portfolio starts with Microsoft at 20%, NVIDIA at 15%, and JPMorgan at 20%. If one holding appreciates much faster than the others, its weight increases automatically while slower-moving positions become relatively smaller.

That creates three questions for the investment team.

How Far Has Each Holding Moved From Target?

The first step is to compare the current reconstructed weight with the original target weight.

A position that moves from 15% to 17% has drifted by +2 percentage points. That is an absolute measure of how much more of the portfolio the holding now represents.

How Large Is the Drift Relative to the Original Allocation?

Absolute drift alone can hide the significance of a move.

For example, a 2 percentage-point change is much more meaningful for a position that started at 5% than for one that started at 25%.

This is why the analysis also calculates relative drift:

Using both measures helps distinguish small allocation noise from changes that materially alter the original portfolio design.

Has the Portfolio Drifted at the Sector Level?

Individual holdings can also shift the portfolio’s sector mix.

If a large Technology position appreciates faster than the rest of the portfolio, the Technology allocation may gradually rise even without any deliberate allocation change.

Sector drift therefore provides a second layer of review beyond individual positions.

Which Holdings Are Driving the Change?

Not every position contributes equally to portfolio drift.

By measuring each holding’s contribution to total absolute drift, Claude can identify whether the portfolio has moved away from target because of:

  • One dominant position;
  • A small group of holdings;
  • Or broader changes across several parts of the portfolio.

The objective is not to rebalance every deviation automatically. It is to identify which changes are large enough to deserve analyst attention before any action is considered.

FMP Data and Claude MCP Setup

To measure portfolio drift, we use a hypothetical $1 million family-office portfolio established on January 2, 2026.

The analysis assumes no trades, deposits, withdrawals, or manual rebalancing after the portfolio is established.

Data Retrieved Through FMP MCP

Claude uses the FMP MCP server to retrieve two types of data for each holding:

  • Company name, sector, and industry;
  • Dividend-adjusted historical prices for January 2 and August 26, 2026.

In the actual run, Claude used FMP:company with profile-symbol for company classifications and FMP:chart with historical-price-eod-dividend-adjusted for the historical price series.

Both dates were valid U.S. trading days, so no substitute dates were required.

Why Dividend-Adjusted Prices Are Used

The analysis treats the change in dividend-adjusted price as a total-return proxy.

For each holding:

The initial allocation is then multiplied by that growth factor:

Once the ending value of every holding is reconstructed, Claude calculates the new portfolio weight:

This is intentionally a simplified no-trade simulation. It does not attempt to reconstruct an actual brokerage account with cash dividends, taxes, transaction costs, or interim portfolio activity.

From Target Weights to Drift

Claude then compares the reconstructed current weights with the original allocation using two measures:

Absolute drift

Relative drift

The same reconstructed weights are also aggregated by FMP sector classification to determine whether portfolio drift is occurring only at the individual-stock level or is also changing the portfolio’s sector allocation.

Measuring Portfolio Drift and Review Thresholds

Once Claude reconstructs the current portfolio weights, the next step is to determine which deviations are large enough to deserve attention.

For this demonstration, we use illustrative review thresholds rather than treating every change as a rebalancing signal.

Position-Level Review Rules

A holding is classified as Within Range when:

  • Absolute drift is below 2 percentage points; and
  • Absolute relative drift is below 15%.

A holding moves to Monitor when it is not already Review Required and either:

  • Absolute drift is between 2 and 4 percentage points; or
  • Absolute relative drift is between 15% and 25%.

A holding is marked Review Required when either:

  • Absolute drift exceeds 4 percentage points; or
  • Absolute relative drift exceeds 25%.

These thresholds are used only to make the example reproducible. They are not universal portfolio-rebalancing standards.

Sector-Level Drift

Claude also aggregates the reconstructed position weights using FMP sector classifications.

For sector exposure, the review bands are:

  • Within Range: absolute drift below 3 percentage points
  • Monitor: 3–5 percentage points
  • Review Required: above 5 percentage points

This provides a second layer of review by showing whether changes in individual holdings are also altering the portfolio’s intended sector mix.

Measuring Overall Portfolio Drift

To summarize how far the entire portfolio has moved from its original allocation, Claude calculates Portfolio Allocation Distance:

Portfolio Allocation Distance = 0.5 × Σ |Current Weight − Target Weight|

This metric captures the aggregate amount of allocation change across all holdings.

We do not assign a Low, Medium, or High label to this value because no classification threshold was defined for it.

Identifying the Main Contributors to Drift

Claude also calculates how much each holding contributes to total absolute drift:

Contribution to Absolute Drift = |Current Weight − Target Weight| ÷ Σ |Current Weight − Target Weight| × 100

This helps distinguish between a portfolio that moved primarily because of one security and one where several holdings gradually shifted away from target.

The objective remains the same throughout: identify deviations that deserve review without automatically converting those deviations into trading instructions.

Running the Analysis with Claude

With the target allocation, drift rules, and review thresholds defined, the next step is to let Claude retrieve the required FMP data and reconstruct the portfolio.

The main prompt asks Claude to use the FMP MCP server to:

  • Retrieve dividend-adjusted prices for the start and end dates;
  • Reconstruct each holding’s ending value;
  • Calculate current portfolio weights;
  • Measure absolute and relative drift;
  • Aggregate the results by sector;
  • Calculate Portfolio Allocation Distance;
  • Identify the holdings contributing most to total drift;
  • Classify positions as Within Range, Monitor, or Review Required.

The full prompt used for the analysis was:

Act as an investment-research analyst supporting a family office.

Using only the Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) MCP server, analyze how far the following hypothetical portfolio has drifted from its original target allocation.

Do not use web search or outside data.

Portfolio:

MSFT — Target Weight: 20% — Initial Allocation: $200,000
NVDA — Target Weight: 15% — Initial Allocation: $150,000
JPM — Target Weight: 20% — Initial Allocation: $200,000
GOOGL — Target Weight: 15% — Initial Allocation: $150,000
XOM — Target Weight: 15% — Initial Allocation: $150,000
JNJ — Target Weight: 15% — Initial Allocation: $150,000

Total portfolio value at inception = $1,000,000.

Assume:
- no trades occurred after the initial allocation;
- no capital was added or withdrawn;
- no manual rebalancing occurred;
- transaction costs, taxes, and cash balances are outside the scope of this demonstration.

Analysis date: August 27, 2026.
Use August 26, 2026, the last completed U.S. trading session, as the ending price date.

Retrieve for each ticker:
- company name;
- sector;
- industry;
- dividend-adjusted historical price for January 2, 2026;
- dividend-adjusted historical price for August 26, 2026.

Use the FMP dividend-adjusted historical price series if available.

If an exact date is unavailable, use the closest valid trading date and state the date actually used.

Do not estimate missing FMP values.

Reconstruct the portfolio using the dividend-adjusted price change as a total-return proxy.

Calculate for each holding:
- growth factor;
- ending value;
- current portfolio weight;
- absolute drift in percentage points;
- relative drift as a percentage of target weight.

Classify each holding using these illustrative rules:

Within Range:
- absolute drift below 2 percentage points; AND
- absolute relative drift below 15%.

Monitor:
- absolute drift between 2 and 4 percentage points inclusive; OR
- absolute relative drift between 15% and 25% inclusive;
- provided Review Required has not already been triggered.

Review Required:
- absolute drift above 4 percentage points; OR
- absolute relative drift above 25%.

Also calculate target and current sector weights using FMP sector classifications.

Classify sector drift as:
- Within Range: below 3 percentage points;
- Monitor: 3–5 percentage points inclusive;
- Review Required: above 5 percentage points.

Calculate Portfolio Allocation Distance as:

0.5 × sum of the absolute position-level weight deviations.

Do not assign a Low, Medium, or High label to this metric.

Also calculate each holding's contribution to total absolute drift.

Based strictly on the calculated evidence, identify:
- the largest overweight;
- the largest underweight;
- Monitor positions;
- Review Required positions;
- the sectors with the largest drift;
- the holdings contributing most to total drift;
- the highest-priority deviations for analyst review.

Do not recommend buying, selling, trimming, adding to, or rebalancing any security.

If important price, sector, or classification data is missing or conflicting, use Review Required rather than guessing.

Do not claim that corporate events were checked unless data capable of verifying them was actually retrieved.

Present the results clearly and concisely using tables where useful.

Include:
- methodology and actual dates used;
- reconstructed portfolio weights;
- position-level drift;
- sector-level drift;
- Portfolio Allocation Distance;
- contribution to total drift;
- key findings;
- Review Required items;
- FMP MCP tools and data types used.

Claude completed the run using dividend-adjusted FMP prices for January 2 and August 26, 2026, with no missing price substitutions required.

The main prompt produced the full quantitative analysis. A narrowly scoped follow-up prompt was then used only to tighten the interpretation without rerunning the FMP retrieval or calculations.

That follow-up removed unsupported qualitative labels around Portfolio Allocation Distance and clarified that single-holding sector drift should not be interpreted as evidence of broader sector or market rotation.

What Claude Found: Which Allocations Drifted the Most

The Claude run reconstructed the portfolio at $1,158,925.10 on August 26, 2026, using FMP dividend-adjusted prices. That represents a 15.89% total-return proxy gain for the no-trade simulation.

More importantly, the analysis showed how uneven performance changed the portfolio’s intended allocation.

JNJ and XOM Moved Furthest Above Target

JNJ became the largest overweight position at 17.12%, or +2.12 percentage points above target.

XOM followed closely at 17.03%, or +2.03 percentage points above target.

Both crossed the 2-percentage-point absolute-drift threshold and were therefore classified as Monitor.

No holding reached the Review Required threshold.

MSFT Became the Largest Underweight

Microsoft moved from a 20% target weight to 18.23%, making it the largest underweight position at -1.77 percentage points.

It remained Within Range because the deviation stayed below both the absolute and relative Monitor thresholds.

This is an important distinction: a holding can post a positive return and still become underweight if other positions appreciate faster.

Overall Allocation Distance Reached 4.15 Percentage Points

Claude calculated a Portfolio Allocation Distance of 4.15 percentage points.

This metric summarizes how far the portfolio moved from its original target allocation across all holdings.

No qualitative label is assigned to the value because the methodology did not define a Low, Medium, or High threshold for Portfolio Allocation Distance.

JNJ and XOM Drove Half of Total Drift

The contribution-to-drift calculation shows which holdings were responsible for most of the allocation change.

JNJ and XOM together accounted for 50% of total absolute drift, while MSFT contributed another 21.35%.

That means most of the change in portfolio structure came from a relatively small number of holdings rather than being distributed evenly across the portfolio.

Sector Drift Stayed Within Range

At the sector level, none of the portfolio’s sectors crossed the 3-percentage-point Monitor threshold.

Technology showed the largest sector-level change at -2.39 percentage points, but still remained Within Range.

However, four of the five sectors contain only one holding in this sample portfolio. Energy is represented only by XOM, Healthcare by JNJ, Financial Services by JPM, and Communication Services by GOOGL.

As a result, drift in those sectors largely reflects the movement of the individual stock rather than a broader sector effect.

The key finding is therefore straightforward: portfolio drift was meaningful enough to flag JNJ and XOM for monitoring, but not large enough to trigger Review Required at either the position or sector level.

When Analyst Intervention Is Required

Portfolio drift can be measured automatically, but the numbers do not always explain why a position moved away from target. Some cases still require analyst review before the result is used in a rebalancing process.

A Threshold Breach Does Not Automatically Mean a Trade

In this example, JNJ and XOM both crossed the 2-percentage-point Monitor threshold.

That tells the investment team that the positions have moved far enough from target to deserve attention. It does not mean either position should automatically be reduced.

The analyst still needs to consider whether the deviation is temporary, expected, or consistent with the portfolio’s current investment policy.

Corporate Events May Explain Large Price Moves

The Claude run used company classifications and dividend-adjusted historical prices. It did not retrieve news, filings, earnings announcements, or other event-level data.

As a result, the analysis does not explain why JNJ or XOM appreciated more than the rest of the portfolio.

If a position shows unusually large drift, an analyst may need to check whether the move was associated with:

  • Earnings or guidance changes;
  • Acquisitions or restructurings;
  • Major corporate actions;
  • Company-specific news;
  • Broader market or sector developments.

These explanations should not be inferred from price data alone.

Single-Holding Sectors Need Careful Interpretation

Four of the five sectors in this sample portfolio contain only one security.

For example, Healthcare exposure is represented entirely by JNJ. Therefore, the portfolio’s +2.12 percentage-point Healthcare drift is mechanically the same as JNJ’s individual drift.

That should not be interpreted as evidence that the Healthcare sector broadly moved in the same direction.

Actual Portfolio Activity Can Break the Simulation

The analysis assumes:

  • No trades;
  • No capital contributions or withdrawals;
  • No manual rebalancing;
  • No separate cash allocation.

If the real portfolio experienced any of these events, reconstructed weights based only on price movements would no longer represent the actual account accurately.

In those cases, the workflow should use actual transaction and holding data rather than infer portfolio evolution from prices alone.

Missing or Conflicting Data Should Trigger Review

Claude should return Review Required rather than estimate when:

  • A required starting or ending price is unavailable;
  • Adjusted-price data is missing;
  • FMP sector classifications are incomplete;
  • Target weights do not reconcile to 100%;
  • Conflicting FMP records appear;
  • A corporate action makes the historical comparison difficult to interpret.

The purpose of the workflow is to make portfolio drift easier to identify and prioritize. The final decision about whether a deviation requires rebalancing still belongs with the investment team.

From Drift Detection to Ongoing Rebalancing Review

A one-time drift analysis is useful, but the more practical family-office use case is to repeat the same review as portfolio weights continue to change.

The same Claude + FMP MCP analysis can be incorporated into a scheduled workflow that compares the latest reconstructed weights with both the original targets and the previous review.

Instead of reproducing the entire portfolio analysis every time, the recurring review can focus on what changed.

Claude can track:

  • Positions that newly moved outside their target range;
  • Positions that moved from Within Range to Monitor;
  • Positions that escalated to Review Required;
  • Previously flagged positions that moved back toward target;
  • Changes in sector-level drift;
  • Changes in Portfolio Allocation Distance;
  • Shifts in which holdings contribute most to total drift.

A simple review status can make the output easier to scan:

  • Within Range
  • Monitor
  • Review Required
  • Resolved

For this demonstration, a weekly review is a reasonable default, with a deeper monthly review for longer-term changes. The cadence can be adjusted based on portfolio turnover, reporting requirements, and how actively the investment team manages allocation ranges.

The recurring workflow could also compare:

Target Allocation → Previous Review → Current Review

This makes it easier to distinguish a temporary deviation from a drift pattern that is continuing to build.

Importantly, the workflow should still stop at review prioritization. Claude can identify that a holding has moved materially away from target, but the decision to rebalance should remain with the investment team.

In this example, the analysis did not produce any Review Required positions. Instead, it identified JNJ and XOM as Monitor items while showing that the rest of the portfolio remained within the defined ranges.

That is exactly the role this workflow is designed to play: not to automate portfolio trading, but to help family-office analysts identify where allocation changes deserve attention before a rebalancing decision is made.
